title: Meditations close

cards: Day five hundred twenty-one, you and i opened a notebook kept by a Roman emperor and started reading it in order. It's easy to dip into a book like this, find a line for a mug, and close it again.
This went the long way: twelve books, a hundred and twenty days, the dull pages along with the well-known ones. Today the notebook closes. Not with a test.
With a question Marcus would ask: what will you actually do with it now?

teach.h: BOOK ONE: THANK-YOUS. BOOK TWELVE: GO.
teach.b: First, the road. Book one is all thank-yous: to his grandfather, his mother, his teachers, his adoptive father, one by one, for what each taught him.
Book two opens with a morning warning: today you'll meet people who are rude, ungrateful, dishonest; they're kin; don't be harmed.

From there the notebook wanders and circles: retreat into yourself; get up and do your work; all is opinion; the view from above; Alexander and his mule driver; and finally, in book twelve, two gates, a small share of time, and an actor leaving the stage at peace.

teach.h: STRAIGHT THROUGH: A PERSON, NOT QUOTES.
teach.b: Second, what reading straight through gives you. The well-known lines sit in context. You see Marcus repeat himself, contradict himself, fall short, try again.
You meet a person, not a quote generator. Third, the Greek word for reading, anagignōskō.

teach.h: ANAGIGNŌSKŌ: TO READ, TO KNOW AGAIN.
teach.b: Dictionaries also give it an older sense: to recognize, to know again. Some readers find that fits this book. Marcus wasn't learning new things in it.
He was recognizing old ones, again. Fourth, what readers do now.
Some who finish the Meditations start over. Some keep a single page open for a season.
Some read one passage every morning, the way Marcus told himself to prepare for the day. There's no wrong way, except treating it as finished.
Tomorrow the path widens: the Stoics who came before Marcus, and the neighbors who argued with them.

games.q: you've just finished all twelve books of the Meditations. what now?
o: pick a passage and read it again, as a daily practice.
games.why: the notebook was practice for Marcus, rules reread until they sank in. finishing it is a start, not an end.

practice: Let one passage from these weeks come to mind first: the morning warning, the inner retreat, all is opinion, the small share of time, the actor leaving the stage.
If the book or a note is nearby, read it once, slowly; if not, say it to yourself in your own words. Notice what it means to you today that it didn't the first time.

wordCard.voice: Know again. The old sense of the Greek word for reading: not learning something new, but recognizing it, to know again. Today's word.
